label: thm:A
title: Theorem A
body_md:
\label{thm:A}
For a two-complex $K$ the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item For every $n\ge1$ there is a chain of two-complexes
$K=K_0\subsetneq K_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq K_n$
in which every inclusion induces the zero map on $\pi_2$.
\item $K$ has a connected acyclic regular cover.
\end{enumerate}
                                                                                                  
                                                                                      
If $K$ is finite and acyclic, the $K_i$ in~\textup{(1)} can be chosen finite.
head: environment

title: Corollary B
body_md:
Let $K$ be the presentation complex of
\[A=\langle x,y\mid x^2yx^{-1}y,\ xy^4xy^{-1}\rangle.\]
Then $\pi_2(K)\cong\mathbb Z^{119}$, and for every $n\ge1$ there is a chain of finite
two-complexes $K=K_0\subsetneq K_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq K_n$ in which every
inclusion is zero on $\pi_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$K$ has one vertex, two edges and two $2$-cells, so its cellular boundary $\partial_1$
vanishes and $\partial_2$ is the exponent-sum matrix
$\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{psmallmatrix}$, of determinant $-1$. Hence $K$ is
acyclic, so it is its own connected acyclic regular cover, and Theorem~A gives the
chains, with finite terms. A coset enumeration shows that $G=\pi_1(K)$ has order
$120$; being perfect, $G$ is $\mathrm{SL}(2,5)$. The universal cover $\widetilde K$ is
simply connected with Euler characteristic $120\,\chi(K)=120$, so
$\pi_2(K)\cong H_2(\widetilde K)\cong\mathbb Z^{119}$.
head: environment

label: lem:toolbox
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:toolbox}
Let $A,X,Y,K,L$ be connected CW-complexes.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item Let $K$ be a two-complex. There is a two-complex $L\supsetneq K$ with
$K\subset L$ zero on $\pi_2$ if and only if $K$ is Cockcroft. If $K$ is finite, $L$ can
be chosen finite.
\item If $A$ is Cockcroft and $f\colon A\to Y$ is trivial on $\pi_1$, then $f$ is zero
on $\pi_2$.
\item Let $f\colon A\to X$ be such that $\pi_2(X)=\mathbb Z[\pi_1X]\cdot f_*\pi_2(A)$. If $A$ is
Cockcroft, so is $X$. If $g\colon X\to Y$ satisfies $g_*f_*=0$ on $\pi_2(A)$, then $g$ is
zero on $\pi_2$.
\item If $g\colon X\to Y$ is injective on $H_2$ and $Y$ is Cockcroft (e.g.\ $Y$ is
aspherical), then $X$ is Cockcroft. A wedge of Cockcroft complexes is Cockcroft.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Let $i\colon K\subset L$ with $L$ a two-complex. Since there are no $3$-cells,
$H_2=\ker\partial_2$ on cellular chains, so $H_2(i)$ is injective. If $i$ is zero on
$\pi_2$, then $H_2(i)\circ h_K=h_L\circ i_*=0$, hence $h_K=0$. Conversely, let $K$ be
Cockcroft. If $\pi_1(K)\ne1$, attach $2$-cells along loops representing a generating
set of $\pi_1(K)$ (finite if $K$ is finite). The resulting $L$ is simply connected, so
$h_L$ is an isomorphism, and $h_L\circ i_*=H_2(i)\circ h_K=0$ gives $i_*=0$. If
$\pi_1(K)=1$, then $h_K$ is an isomorphism and zero, so $\pi_2(K)=0$, and we may take
$L=K\cup e^1\cup e^2$ with $e^2$ attached along the loop $e^1$.

(b) By the lifting criterion, $f$ lifts to $\tilde f\colon A\to\widetilde Y$, and
$f_*=p_*\tilde f_*$ where $p\colon\widetilde Y\to Y$ is the covering. Now
$h_{\widetilde Y}\tilde f_*=H_2(\tilde f)h_A=0$, and $h_{\widetilde Y}$ is an
isomorphism, so $\tilde f_*=0$.

(c) The Hurewicz map is invariant under the action of $\pi_1$, so
$h_X(\gamma\cdot f_*s)=h_X(f_*s)=H_2(f)h_A(s)=0$ for $\gamma\in\pi_1X$, $s\in\pi_2A$.
Similarly $g_*(\gamma\cdot f_*s)=g_*(\gamma)\cdot g_*f_*s=0$.

(d) We have $H_2(g)\circ h_X=h_Y\circ g_*=0$ and $H_2(g)$ is injective, so $h_X=0$.
For a wedge $W=\bigvee_rX_r$ with retractions $\rho_r\colon W\to X_r$, the map
$H_2(W)\to\prod_rH_2(X_r)$ with coordinates $H_2(\rho_r)$ is injective, and
$H_2(\rho_r)h_W=h_{X_r}\rho_{r*}=0$.
head: environment

label: prop:fox
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$K_N$ has no $3$-cells, so $H_2=\ker\partial_2$; and
$H_1(K_N)=\pi_1(K_N)^{\mathrm{ab}}=N/[N,N]$.
head: environment

label: rem:fox
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:fox}
If $K$ has a single vertex, it is the presentation complex of a presentation
$\langle x_i\ (i\in I)\mid r_j\ (j\in J)\rangle$ of $G$, and $\partial_N$ is right
multiplication by the matrix $\bigl(\overline{\partial r_j/\partial x_i}\bigr)$ of Fox
derivatives, reduced to $\mathbb Z[G/N]$ \cite{Fox}, \cite[Ch.~II, \S3]{LyndonSchupp}. For
$N=G$ this is the exponent-sum matrix. Every two-complex is homotopy equivalent to such
a complex, by collapsing a maximal tree of its $1$-skeleton.
head: environment

label: lem:components
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:components}
Let $K\subset X$ be connected CW-complexes and let $M$ be the kernel of
$\pi_1(K)\to\pi_1(X)$. Then every component of the preimage of $K$ in $\widetilde X$ is
a copy of $K_M$, and $\pi_1(X)$ permutes these components transitively.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The preimage of $K$ is a covering space of $K$. A loop in $K$ lifts to a loop in
$\widetilde X$ if and only if it is trivial in $\pi_1(X)$, so the component through a
base lift is the cover with fundamental group $M$. The deck group acts transitively on
the fibre over the base point, hence on the components.
head: environment

label: lem:coinv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coinv}
Let $H$ be a torsion-free abelian normal subgroup of a group $Q$, and let
$f\colon U\to V$ be a homomorphism of free left $k[Q]$-modules of arbitrary ranks.
If $k[Q/H]\otimes_{k[Q]}f$ is injective, then $f$ is injective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Restrict scalars to $R=k[H]$. Since $k[Q]$ is a free $R$-module on a set of coset
representatives, $U$ and $V$ are free $R$-modules. Let $\varepsilon\colon R\to k$ be the
augmentation, with kernel $I_H$. As $H$ is normal, $k[Q/H]\otimes_{k[Q]}U\cong U/I_HU
\cong k\otimes_RU$, and under these identifications $k[Q/H]\otimes f$ becomes
$k\otimes_Rf$. The ring $R$ is a commutative domain: every finite computation in $R$
takes place in the Laurent polynomial ring $k[t_1^{\pm1},\dots,t_s^{\pm1}]$ of a finitely
generated, hence free abelian, subgroup of~$H$.

\emph{Claim.} If $v_1,\dots,v_m\in V$ have $k$-linearly independent images
$\bar v_1,\dots,\bar v_m$ in $k\otimes_RV$, then they are $R$-linearly independent.

We induct on $m$, the case $m=0$ being empty. Since $\bar v_1\ne0$, some coordinate
functional $\lambda\colon V\to R$ with respect to an $R$-basis of $V$ satisfies
$\varepsilon(a)\ne0$, where $a:=\lambda(v_1)$; in particular $a\ne0$. Put
$w_j=av_j-\lambda(v_j)v_1$ for $2\le j\le m$. Their images
$\varepsilon(a)\bar v_j-\varepsilon(\lambda(v_j))\bar v_1$ are $k$-linearly independent,
because the $\bar v_j$ are and $\varepsilon(a)\ne0$ in the domain~$k$. By induction the
$w_j$ are $R$-linearly independent. If $\sum_jc_jv_j=0$ with $c_j\in R$, then, $R$
being commutative,
\[
0=a\sum_jc_jv_j-\lambda\Bigl(\sum_jc_jv_j\Bigr)v_1=\sum_{j\ge2}c_jw_j ,
\]
so $c_j=0$ for $j\ge2$. Then $c_1v_1=0$, and applying $\lambda$ gives $c_1a=0$, so $c_1=0$.

Now let $(e_\alpha)$ be an $R$-basis of $U$. The $\bar e_\alpha$ form a $k$-basis of
$k\otimes_RU$, so by injectivity of $k\otimes_Rf$ every finite subfamily of
$(\overline{f(e_\alpha)})$ is $k$-linearly independent. By the claim, every finite
subfamily of $(f(e_\alpha))$ is $R$-linearly independent, i.e.\ $f$ is injective.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{test} is a pair $(k,v)$ with $k\in\{\mathbb Z\}\cup\{\mathbb F_p:p\text{ prime}\}$ and
$v\in k[G]^{(J)}$. A normal subgroup $M\trianglelefteq G$ \emph{passes} the test
$(k,v)$ if $\partial_M(v_M)=0$ implies $v_M=0$; otherwise it \emph{fails} it. We call
$M$ \emph{good} if it passes every test.
head: environment

label: lem:pigeon
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:pigeon}
Let $K=X_0\subset X_1\subset\cdots\subset X_m$ be a chain of two-complexes in which every
inclusion is zero on $\pi_2$, and let $M_r=\ker(G\to\pi_1X_r)$, so that
$1=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_m$. For every test $(k,v)$ and
$0\le r<m$,
\[
\partial_{M_r}(v_{M_r})=0\ \Longrightarrow\ v_{M_{r+1}}=0 .
\]
Consequently each test is failed by at most one $M_r$, and any $m$ tests are all passed
by some $M_r$ with $0\le r\le m$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $r<m$ and write $X=X_r$, $X'=X_{r+1}$, $M=M_r$, $M'=M_{r+1}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:components}, the components of the preimages of $K$ in $\widetilde X$
and $\widetilde X'$ through the base points are copies of $K_M$ and $K_{M'}$, and the
based lift $\widetilde X\to\widetilde X'$ of the inclusion restricts to the covering map
$K_M\to K_{M'}$. On $2$-chains, the latter is the reduction
$k[G/M]^{(J)}\to k[G/M']^{(J)}$.

Assume $\partial_M(v_M)=0$. Then $v_M$ is a $2$-cycle of $K_M\subset\widetilde X$, and
its image $v_{M'}$ is a $2$-cycle of $\widetilde X'$. The map
$H_2(\widetilde X;k)\to H_2(\widetilde X';k)$ is zero: for $k=\mathbb Z$ it is the map
$\pi_2(X)\to\pi_2(X')$; for $k=\mathbb F_p$, since $H_1(\widetilde X)=H_1(\widetilde X')=0$,
the universal coefficient theorem identifies it naturally with
$(\pi_2(X)\to\pi_2(X'))\otimes\mathbb F_p=0$. Thus $v_{M'}$ is a null-homologous $2$-cycle in a
complex without $3$-cells, so $v_{M'}=0$.

If a test fails at $r$, then $v_{M_{r+1}}=0$, hence $v_{M_s}=0$ for all $s>r$ (as
$M_{r+1}\subseteq M_s$), so it passes at every $s>r$. Applying this to the smallest
index where the test fails shows that it fails at most once. Since $m$ tests have at
most $m$ failures among the $m+1$ indices, some index is failed by none.
head: environment

label: lem:compact
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Identify subsets of $G$ with points of the compact space $\{0,1\}^G$; the normal
subgroups form a closed subset $\mathcal N$. Fix a test $(k,v)$, and let $S\subset G$ be
a finite set containing the supports of all coordinates of $v$ and of $\partial_1v$.
Since $v_M$ and $\partial_M(v_M)=(\partial_1v)_M$ are obtained by summing coefficients
over left cosets $sM$, and $sM=s'M$ if and only if $s^{-1}s'\in M$, whether $M$ passes
$(k,v)$ depends only on $M\cap S^{-1}S$. Hence the set $\mathcal N_{(k,v)}$ of normal
subgroups passing $(k,v)$ is clopen in $\mathcal N$. By hypothesis~(1) and
Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon}, applied to a chain of length $m$, any $m$ of the sets
$\mathcal N_{(k,v)}$ have a common point. By compactness,
$\mathcal G=\bigcap_{(k,v)}\mathcal N_{(k,v)}$ is nonempty, and it is closed.

If $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal G$ is totally ordered by inclusion, then
$\bigcap\mathcal C$ is the limit in $\{0,1\}^G$ of the net $\mathcal C$, ordered by
reverse inclusion: for each $g\in G$, membership of $g$ is eventually constant and equal
to membership in $\bigcap\mathcal C$. Hence $\bigcap\mathcal C\in\mathcal G$, and Zorn's
lemma gives a minimal element.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N$ be a minimal element of $\mathcal G$. Then $H_2(K_N;k)=0$ for $k=\mathbb Z$ and every
$k=\mathbb F_p$. By the universal coefficient theorem,
$\mathrm{Tor}(H_1(K_N),\mathbb F_p)\subseteq H_2(K_N;\mathbb F_p)=0$ for every $p$, so
$H_1(K_N)=N/[N,N]$ is torsion-free.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:coinv} with $Q=G/[N,N]$, $H=N/[N,N]$ and $f=\partial_{[N,N]}$ over
$k$. Since $C_*(K_N;k)=k[G/N]\otimes_{k[Q]}C_*(K_{[N,N]};k)$, we have
$k[Q/H]\otimes_{k[Q]}f=\partial_N$, which is injective. Hence $\partial_{[N,N]}$ is
injective over every $k$, i.e.\ $[N,N]\in\mathcal G$. Minimality gives $[N,N]=N$. Thus
$H_1(K_N)=0$ and $H_2(K_N)=0$, and $K_N$ is a connected acyclic regular cover of~$K$.
head: environment
name: Proof of $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$

label: prop:descent
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:descent}
Let $D=L_0\subsetneq L_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq L_n$ be two-complexes with all
inclusions zero on $\pi_2$, such that $\pi_1(D)\to\pi_1(L_i)$ is trivial for $i\ge1$.
Let $E_i=K\cup_pL_i$ be the pushout of $K\xleftarrow{p}D\subset L_i$, i.e.\ $K$
together with the cells of $L_i\smallsetminus D$, attached by composing their attaching
maps with $p$ on~$D$. Then $K=E_0\subsetneq E_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq E_n$ are
two-complexes and all inclusions are zero on $\pi_2$. If $K$ and all $L_i$ are finite,
so are all~$E_i$.
head: environment
name: Descent

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Cells and $\pi_1$.} The cells of $E_i$ are those of $K$ and those of
$L_i\smallsetminus D$, so the $E_i$ are strictly nested two-complexes. Put
$\Pi_i=\pi_1(L_i)$. By van Kampen's theorem $\pi_1(E_i)$ is the pushout of
$G\leftarrow\pi_1(D)\rightarrow\Pi_i$. The first map has normal image $N$ and the second
is trivial, so
\[
\Lambda_i:=\pi_1(E_i)=(G/N)*\Pi_i=H*\Pi_i .
\]

\emph{$\pi_2$ is generated from $L_i$.} Write $\Lambda=\Lambda_i$ and $\Pi=\Pi_i$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:components}, in $\widetilde E_i$: the preimage of $K$ is a disjoint union
of copies of $K_N=D$ indexed by $\Lambda/H$ (the kernel of $G\to\Lambda$ is $N$, since
$H$ embeds in $H*\Pi$); the preimage of $L_i$ is a disjoint union of copies of
$\widetilde L_i$ indexed by $\Lambda/\Pi$; and the preimage of $D$ is a disjoint union
of copies of $D$ indexed by $\Lambda$, as $\pi_1(D)$ dies in $\Lambda$. These are
subcomplexes, the first two cover $\widetilde E_i$ and intersect in the third, so we
have a short exact sequence of cellular chain complexes
\[
0\to\bigoplus_{\Lambda}C_*(D)\to\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\Lambda/H}C_*(D)\Bigr)\oplus
\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\Lambda/\Pi}C_*(\widetilde L_i)\Bigr)\to C_*(\widetilde E_i)\to0 .
\]
Since $H_1(D)=H_2(D)=0$, the long exact homology sequence gives an isomorphism
$\bigoplus_{\Lambda/\Pi}H_2(\widetilde L_i)\to H_2(\widetilde E_i)$, that is,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:descent-pi2}
\mathbb Z[\Lambda]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[\Pi]}\pi_2(L_i)\ \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\ \pi_2(E_i),
\end{equation}
induced by $L_i\to E_i$. In particular
$\pi_2(E_i)=\mathbb Z[\Lambda]\cdot\operatorname{im}\pi_2(L_i)$.

\emph{Zero maps.} The covering $p$ is bijective on $\pi_2$, and the composite
$D\xrightarrow{p}K\subset E_1$ equals $D\subset L_1\to E_1$, which is zero on $\pi_2$;
hence $K\subset E_1$ is zero on $\pi_2$. For $i\ge1$, the square formed by
$L_i\subset L_{i+1}$ and $E_i\subset E_{i+1}$ commutes, its top arrow is zero on
$\pi_2$, and $\pi_2(E_i)$ is generated by the image of $\pi_2(L_i)$; so
$E_i\subset E_{i+1}$ is zero on $\pi_2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(c).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:relative} to the acyclic cover $D$ and then
Proposition~\ref{prop:descent}. If $K$ is finite and acyclic, take $D=K$ and $p$ the
identity; then $E_i=L_i$, which are finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:relative}.
head: environment
name: Proof of $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$, given Proposition~\ref{prop:relative}

label: prop:relative
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:relative}
Let $D$ be an acyclic two-complex and $n\ge1$. There are two-complexes
\[
D=L_0\subsetneq L_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq L_n
\]
with all inclusions zero on $\pi_2$ and $\pi_1(D)\to\pi_1(L_i)$ trivial for $i\ge1$.
If $D$ is finite, all $L_i$ can be chosen finite.
head: environment

label: lem:initial
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{The group.} Eliminate $x_i=U_i:=[a_i,b_i]$. The cross-commutators make the
subgroups $\langle a_i,b_i\rangle$ commute pairwise, so the $U_i$ commute, and $r_j$ becomes
$r_j(U)=\prod_iU_i^{\Theta_{ij}}$. For $c=\Theta^{-1}e_i\in\mathbb Z^{(J)}$ we get
\[
U_i=\prod_jr_j(U)^{c_j}=1 .
\]
So $x_i=1$ and all $a_i,b_i$ commute. Conversely, sending $a_i,b_i$ to a basis of the
free abelian group on $\{a_i,b_i\}$ and $x_i$ to $0$ satisfies every relator.

\emph{Cockcroft.} Eliminating the $x_i$ by the relators $x_iU_i^{-1}$ is a Tietze
transformation, hence a homotopy equivalence \cite[Ch.~I]{HMS}, from $Y_D/\mathcal T_D$
to the presentation complex $Y'$ with generators $a_i,b_i$ and relators $r_j(U)$ and the
cross-commutators. All these relators have zero exponent sums, so the cellular boundary
$\partial_2$ of $Y'$ vanishes and $H_2(Y')$ is free on the $2$-cells. Let $\mathbb T$ be
the union of the finite subtori of $\prod_{i\in I}(S^1_{a_i}\times S^1_{b_i})$, with its
product cell structure. It is a $K(\mathbb Z^{(2I)},1)$, and $H_2(\mathbb T)$ is free on the
coordinate squares. Map $Y'\to\mathbb T$ by sending generators to the corresponding
circles, each cross-commutator disk onto its square with degree one, and the disk of
$r_j(U)$, whose boundary is a concatenation of loops $U_i^{\pm1}$, onto the
concatenation of the corresponding $(a_i,b_i)$-squares. On $H_2$:
\[
[r_j(U)]\longmapsto\sum_i\Theta_{ij}\,[(a_i,b_i)\text{-square}],
\qquad[\text{cross-commutator}]\longmapsto[\text{its square}].
\]
A class in the kernel has zero cross-commutator coefficients, and its vector
$\lambda\in\mathbb Z^{(J)}$ of remaining coefficients satisfies $\Theta\lambda=0$, so
$\lambda=0$. Thus $H_2(Y')\to H_2(\mathbb T)$ is injective, and $Y'\simeq Y_D$ is
Cockcroft by Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(d).

\emph{The inclusion.} $D\subset Y_D$ is trivial on $\pi_1$, as $\pi_1(D)$ is generated by
the $x_i$, and $D$ is Cockcroft since $H_2(D)=0$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(b).
head: environment

label: thm:blocks
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:blocks}
For every $q\ge1$ there is a finite presentation
\[B_q=\langle s_1,t_1,\dots,s_q,t_q,Z_q\mid\beta_{q,1},\dots,\beta_{q,m_q}\rangle,\]
with $m_q\ge1$ and $Z_q$ a finite list of \emph{internal} generators, such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\normalfont\bfseries(B\arabic*)},leftmargin=14mm]
\item\label{B1} \emph{Marking.} There is a cellular map $b_q\colon\Sigma_q\toK(B_q)$
sending each edge to the generator of the same name.
\item\label{B2} \emph{Replacement creates no new $\pi_2$.} Let $E=\langle X\mid R,r\rangle$ be a
presentation, and suppose $r=\prod_{h=1}^q[u_h,v_h]$ in the free group on $X$. Replace
the relator $r$ by a block with fresh internal generators $Z_r$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:replace}
E'=\langle X,Z_r\mid R,\ \beta_{q,j}(u_1,v_1,\dots,u_q,v_q,Z_r)\ (1\le j\le m_q)\rangle .
\end{equation}
Let $f\colonK(E)\toK(E')$ be the \emph{structural map}: the identity on the
$1$-skeleton of $K(E)$ and on the $2$-cells of $R$, and on the $2$-cell $r$ the
filling of $\prod_h[u_h,v_h]$ given by $b_q$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-generation}
\pi_2(E')=\mathbb Z[G(E')]\cdot f_*\pi_2(E).
\end{equation}
The same holds for the simultaneous replacement of any set of relators, each with its
own fresh internal generators.
\item\label{B3} \emph{Capped blocks are Cockcroft.} The presentation
$\langle Z_q\mid\beta_{q,j}(1,\dots,1,Z_q)\ (1\le j\le m_q)\rangle$ is Cockcroft.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Blocks

label: lem:structural
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $f\colon A\to B$ and $g\colon B\to C$ satisfy the generation property
$\pi_2(B)=\mathbb Z[\pi_1B]\cdot f_*\pi_2(A)$ and similarly for $g$, then so does $gf$,
because $g_*(\gamma s)=g_*(\gamma)\,g_*(s)$. It therefore suffices to check generation for
each rule.

\emph{Rule 1.} Let $P_1'$ be obtained from $P$ by adding, for each extra generator $z$,
a loop $b_z$, a loop $a_z$ and a $2$-cell along $a_zb_za_z^{-1}(zb_z)^{-1}$. This relator
says $z=[a_z,b_z]$, and eliminating each $z$ by it is a Tietze transformation
\cite[Ch.~I]{HMS}, giving the presentation of rule~1; under this homotopy equivalence the
inclusion $P\subset P_1'$ becomes the map of rule~1. Now $P_1'$ is a graph of spaces
\cite{ScottWall}: the vertex space is $P\vee\bigvee_zS^1_{b_z}$, and each new $2$-cell
together with $a_z$ is a cylinder $S^1\times[0,1]$ glued along $b_z$ and $zb_z$. Both
loops have infinite order in $G(P)*F(\{b_z\})$, as is seen by killing $G(P)$. So
$G(P_1')$ is an HNN extension along infinite cyclic subgroups, in which the vertex group
embeds \cite[Ch.~IV, \S2]{LyndonSchupp}. Consequently $\widetilde{P_1'}$ is a tree of
spaces whose vertex spaces $V_\alpha$ are copies of the universal cover of
$P\vee\bigvee_zS^1$ and whose edge spaces are strips $\mathbb R\times[0,1]$. Since
$H_*(\mathbb R\times[0,1],\mathbb R\times\{0,1\})$ is concentrated in degree~$1$,
excision gives $H_2(\widetilde{P_1'},\bigsqcup_\alpha V_\alpha)=0$, so
$\bigoplus_\alpha H_2(V_\alpha)\to H_2(\widetilde{P_1'})$ is onto. By the same argument
applied to the wedge with circles (a tree of copies of $\widetilde P$ joined by lines),
each $H_2(V_\alpha)$ is generated by translates of $\pi_2(P)$.

\emph{Rule 2.} The attaching maps of $r^*$ and $r^0$ are homotopic in the complex
obtained by removing all extra relator cells, since the correcting word is null-homotopic
in $D$. Hence the map of rule~2 is a homotopy equivalence \cite[Prop.~0.18]{Hatcher}.

\emph{Rule 3.} This is exactly \ref{B2}.

The consequences follow from~\eqref{eq:generation} and Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(c): if
$P$ is Cockcroft, so is $T(P)$; and if $j_*=0$ on $\pi_2$, then
$T(j)_*\eta_{P*}=\eta_{P'*}j_*=0$, so $T(j)_*=0$.
head: environment

label: lem:terminal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:terminal}
Suppose that $P$ is Cockcroft and that all core generators $x_i$ are trivial in $G(P)$.
Then the $x_i$ are trivial in $G(T(P))$ and $G(T^{+}(P))$, the inclusion
$T(P)\subsetT^{+}(P)$ is zero on $\pi_2$, and $T^{+}(P)$ is Cockcroft.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The $x_i$ remain trivial because $\eta_P$ fixes them.

\emph{The inclusion.} The composite $P\to T(P)\subsetT^{+}(P)$ is trivial on $\pi_1$: the
$x_i$ are trivial by hypothesis, and each extra generator $z$ maps to $[a_z,b_z]$, a
commutator of two capped loops. Since $P$ is Cockcroft, the composite is zero on $\pi_2$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(b). By~\eqref{eq:generation} and Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(c),
the inclusion $T(P)\subsetT^{+}(P)$ is zero on $\pi_2$.

\emph{Cockcroft.} Since $D$ is acyclic, the quotient map
$\kappa\colonT^{+}(P)\toT^{+}(P)/D$ is an isomorphism on $H_2$ (long exact sequence of the
pair). In $T^{+}(P)/D$, all $x_i$ and core relators have disappeared, and the remaining
cells are the loops $a_z,b_z$ with their capping disks, and the blocks. Eliminating the
$a_z,b_z$ by their capping disks is a homotopy equivalence \cite[Ch.~I]{HMS}. As the words
$u_h,v_h$ only involve the $x_i$ and the $a_z,b_z$, every block relator
$\beta_{q,j}(u,v,Z_r)$ becomes $\beta_{q,j}(1,\dots,1,Z_r)$, and distinct blocks have
disjoint internal generators. Therefore
\[
T^{+}(P)/D\ \simeq\ \bigvee_rK(\langle Z_r\mid\beta_{q(r),j}(1,\dots,1,Z_r)\ (1\le j\le m_{q(r)})\rangle) ,
\]
the wedge being over the extra relators $r$ of $P$. Each wedge summand is Cockcroft by
\ref{B3}, hence so is the wedge (Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(d)), and $T^{+}(P)$ is Cockcroft
by Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(d) applied to~$\kappa$.

label: lem:spine
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:spine}\
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},itemsep=2pt]
\item $C_q=M_q\cup_{\Sigma_q}\operatorname{Cone}(\Sigma_q)$ is a finite $3$-dimensional cube complex all
of whose vertex links are isomorphic to $L_q$. It is aspherical.
\item $M_q$ collapses onto a finite two-dimensional subcomplex.
\item The inclusion $\Sigma_q\subset M_q$ maps the fundamental class $[\Sigma_q]$ to $0$ in
$H_2(M_q)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) This follows from the discussion above, as $\dim L_q=2$.

                                                                                                   
(iii) Since $L_q$ is a closed surface, every edge $\tau$ of $L_q$ lies in exactly two
triangles; hence every square of $C_q$ lies in exactly two $3$-cubes. Orient $\Sigma_q$,
and let $o(\sigma)=\pm1$ compare the orientation of a triangle $\sigma$ with the one given
by increasing order of its vertices. Orient each cube $[-1,1]^\sigma\times\{\epsilon\}$
by increasing order of coordinates, and give it the coefficient
$o(\sigma)\prod_{h\notin\sigma}\epsilon_h$. Let a square $[-1,1]^\tau\times\{\eta\}$ lie
in the cubes indexed by $\sigma_i=\tau\cup\{k_i\}$, $i=1,2$, and let $p_i$ be the number
of elements of $\tau$ smaller than $k_i$. The square appears in the boundary of the
$i$-th cube with coefficient $\eta_{k_1}\eta_{k_2}E\cdot o(\sigma_i)(-1)^{p_i}$, where
$E=\prod_{h\notin\sigma_1\cup\sigma_2}\eta_h$; and $o(\sigma_1)(-1)^{p_1}+o(\sigma_2)(-1)^{p_2}=0$
because $\tau$ cancels in the fundamental cycle of $\Sigma_q$. So these coefficients
define a $3$-cycle $\zeta$ of $C_q$. Now consider the exact sequence
\[
H_3(C_q)\to H_3(C_q,M_q)\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }H_2(M_q).
\]
By excision $H_3(C_q,M_q)\cong H_3(\operatorname{Cone}\Sigma_q,\Sigma_q)\cong H_2(\Sigma_q)\cong\mathbb Z$,
and under this identification $\delta$ becomes the map induced by $\Sigma_q\subset M_q$.
The cubes containing $v$ are those with all signs $+1$, and their coefficients in
$\zeta$ are the $o(\sigma)$; so $\zeta$ maps to a generator of $H_3(C_q,M_q)$. Hence
$\delta=0$, and $[\Sigma_q]\mapsto0$.

(ii) $M_q$ is a polyhedral complex whose $3$-cells are the cubes of $C_q$, those
containing $v$ being truncated. Consider the graph whose vertices are these $3$-cells,
two being adjacent when they share a $2$-cell. It is connected: the cubes containing a
given vertex $w\in\{\pm1\}^d$ correspond to the triangles of $L_q$, and are connected
because $L_q$ is a connected closed surface; and two vertices $w,w'$ differing in one
coordinate $k$ lie in a common cube, namely any cube indexed by a triangle containing
$k$. Choose a spanning tree, rooted at a truncated cube. A triangle of the cut surface
lies in only one $3$-cell, so we can collapse the root across it. Then collapse each other
$3$-cell, in order of distance to the root, across the $2$-cell it shares with its parent:
that $2$-cell lies in exactly two $3$-cells and the parent has been removed, so it is a
free face. All $3$-cells disappear.

label: lem:geometric-pushout
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:geometric-pushout}
Let $X$ be a two-complex, $a\colon\Sigma_q\to X$ a cellular map, and
$W=X\cup_a(\Sigma_q\times[0,1])\cup_{\Sigma_q}M_q$, where $\Sigma_q\times\{0\}$ is glued
to $X$ by $a$ and $\Sigma_q\times\{1\}$ to the cut surface of $M_q$. Then
$\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(W)$ is injective, and $\pi_2(W)$ is generated over $\mathbb Z[\pi_1W]$ by the
image of $\pi_2(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Collapsing $X$ to a point turns $\Sigma_q\times[0,1]$ into $\operatorname{Cone}(\Sigma_q)$, so
$W/X=C_q$; let $\kappa\colon W\to C_q$ be the quotient map. It is a homeomorphism from
$W\smallsetminus X$ onto $C_q\smallsetminus\{v\}$.

                                                                                        
\emph{Step 1: $\pi_1$-injectivity (cf.\ \cite[Lemma~2.2]{DJW}).} Let
$\widehat W\to W$ be the pullback of the universal cover $\widetilde C_q\to C_q$ along
$\kappa$. It is obtained from $\widetilde C_q$ by replacing each lift $v_\lambda$ of $v$,
together with its open cone neighbourhood, by a copy
$X_\lambda\cup_a(\Sigma_q\times[0,1])$; in particular it is connected. Fix a lift $v_0$.
Since $\widetilde C_q$ is CAT(0), each point $y$ outside the open cone neighbourhood of
$v_0$ is joined to $v_0$ by a unique geodesic, which crosses the cut surface
$\Sigma_{(0)}$ at $v_0$ exactly once (inside each cube at $v_0$ geodesics from $v_0$ are
straight segments, and the cut is an affine hyperplane). Mapping $y$ to this crossing
point defines a retraction $\rho$ onto $\Sigma_{(0)}\cong\Sigma_q$, continuous because
geodesics in CAT(0) spaces depend continuously on their endpoints. Define
$R\colon\widehat W\to X_0=X$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item on the lift of $M_q$, $R=a\circ\rho$;
\item on $X_0$, $R$ is the identity, and on its cylinder $R(\sigma,t)=a(\sigma)$;
\item at $\lambda\ne0$: $\rho$ is defined on the whole closed cone neighbourhood of
$v_\lambda$, so its restriction to the cut surface $\Sigma_{(\lambda)}\cong\Sigma_q$
extends over a cone and is therefore homotopic to a constant map by a homotopy
$H\colon\Sigma_q\times[0,1]\to\Sigma_q$ with $H_1=\rho|_{\Sigma_{(\lambda)}}$ and $H_0$
constant. Put $R(\sigma,t)=a(H(\sigma,t))$ on the cylinder and let $R$ be constant on
$X_\lambda$.
\end{itemize}
These definitions agree on overlaps, so $R$ is a retraction of $\widehat W$ onto $X_0$.
Hence $\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(\widehat W)$ is injective, and so is
$\pi_1(\widehat W)\to\pi_1(W)$; their composite is induced by $X\subset W$.

\emph{Step 2: a CAT(0) quotient (cf.\ \cite[Lemma~2.6]{DJW}).} Let $U\subset\widetilde W$
be the preimage of $X$. By Step~1 and Lemma~\ref{lem:components}, its components
$U_\alpha$ are copies of $\widetilde X$. Collapse each $U_\alpha$ to a point $v_\alpha$
to obtain a space $V$, and let $V_0=\{v_\alpha\}$. As $\widetilde W$ is simply connected
and the $U_\alpha$ are disjoint connected subcomplexes, $V\simeq\widetilde W\cup\bigcup_\alpha\operatorname{Cone}(U_\alpha)$
\cite[Ch.~0]{Hatcher} is simply connected by van Kampen's theorem. The cylinders
attached to $U_\alpha$ become cones with apex $v_\alpha$, and each truncated cube together
with the cone on its cut triangle becomes a full cube; so $V$ is a cube complex. The
vertex links at old vertices are copies of $L_q$. The link at $v_\alpha$ is the preimage
in $\widetilde W$ of the cut surface adjacent to $U_\alpha$, that is, the pullback of
$\widetilde X\to X$ along $a$: a disjoint union of covers of $L_q$. Covers of $L_q$ are
flag: the vertices of a clique in a cover project to pairwise adjacent, hence distinct,
vertices of $L_q$, which span a simplex; this simplex lifts to a simplex through any
vertex of the clique, and since a covering map is an isomorphism on the star of a vertex,
the lift contains the whole clique. Hence $V$ is CAT(0) (by \cite{Leary}, as $V$ need not
be locally finite), so contractible.

\emph{Step 3: homology.} Since $(\widetilde W,U)\to(V,V_0)$ is a relative homeomorphism
of CW pairs and $V_0$ is discrete,
$H_2(\widetilde W,U)\cong H_2(V,V_0)\cong H_2(V)=0$. Hence
$H_2(U)\to H_2(\widetilde W)$ is surjective. By Lemma~\ref{lem:components}, $\pi_1(W)$
permutes the components of $U$ transitively, and the component through the base point
is a copy of $\widetilde X$ with $H_2=\pi_2(X)$. Since $\pi_2(W)=H_2(\widetilde W)$, it
is generated over $\mathbb Z[\pi_1W]$ by the image of $\pi_2(X)$.

label: lem:capped-block
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By homotopy invariance, $C_q=M_q\cup_{\Sigma_q}\operatorname{Cone}(\Sigma_q)\simeq
K(B_q)\cup_{b_q}\operatorname{Cone}(\Sigma_q)$. With the one-vertex structure on $\Sigma_q$, the cone
consists of the cone point, an edge (the cone on the vertex), $2$-cells (the cones on
$s_h,t_h$) and one $3$-cell $e^3$ (the cone on the polygon). Contracting the edge
\cite[Prop.~0.17]{Hatcher} gives $C_q\simeq V_q\cup e^3$.

The cellular boundary of $e^3$ consists of the $2$-chain $b_{q\#}[\Sigma_q]$ on
$K(B_q)$, and of the capping $2$-cells with coefficients the exponent sums of $s_h$
and $t_h$ in $\omega_q$, which vanish. The chain $b_{q\#}[\Sigma_q]$ is a $2$-cycle of
$K(B_q)$ representing the image of $[\Sigma_q]$, which is zero by
Lemma~\ref{lem:spine}(iii) since $b_q$ corresponds to the inclusion
$\Sigma_q\subset M_q$. A null-homologous $2$-cycle in a two-complex is the zero chain,
so $\partial e^3=0$, and $H_2(V_q)\to H_2(V_q\cup e^3)$ is an isomorphism. As
$V_q\cup e^3\simeq C_q$ is aspherical, $V_q$ is Cockcroft by
Lemma~\ref{lem:toolbox}(d). Finally, eliminating each $s_h,t_h$ by its capping
$2$-cell is a homotopy equivalence from $V_q$ to the presentation complex of the capped
presentation $\langle Z_q\mid\beta_{q,j}(1,\dots,1,Z_q)\rangle$.
